solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Celeb, a co-star being silly in fun run (8,4)

indicators.note: Letters that are being silly are messing about rather than standing in their proper order.

annotation.surface: A famous name and a fellow actor clown about in a charity fun run.
annotation.walkthrough: The celebrity-in-a-charity-run picture makes "Celeb, a co-star" read as people rather than twelve letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a race over hurdles, nets and mud is the classic comic event of a charity fun run.

entries.clue: Plant beginning to beat, say, competition (9)

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is its first letter, so only the opening B of 'beat' is used.

blocks.note: a cup is a competition, like the FA Cup

annotation.surface: A plant sets out to win a contest.
annotation.walkthrough: "say" looks like the throwaway 'for example', but it is a verb supplying UTTER.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: the buttercup is one particular yellow-flowered wild plant.

entries.clue: Anxiety is seen in group of nine, all retreating (7)

indicators.note: Something seen in another thing sits inside it, so IS goes within the other letters.
Retreating means going backwards, so the combined letters are read in reverse.

blocks.note: a nonet is a group of nine musicians
as written, placed after the first two letters to make NO-IS-NET

annotation.surface: A band of nine players all back away nervously.
annotation.walkthrough: "all" tells you that everything built so far, IS included, runs backwards, not just the group of nine.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: nervous strain and anxiety are the same state of mind.

entries.clue: Price demanded is a burden (6)

blocks.note: a load or duty laid on someone

annotation.surface: A complaint that a cost is too heavy to bear.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as a grumble, the clue hides that each half defines the answer on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: the sum asked for a service, and an old sense of a load or responsibility laid upon someone.

entries.clue: Communication, the reverse of feeble, engaging one (5)

indicators.note: The reverse of a word is that word written backwards.
To engage something is to take it in and hold it, so these letters wrap round the next piece.

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one, held between the third and fourth letters

annotation.surface: A message that is anything but weak, drawing someone in.
annotation.walkthrough: "engaging" reads as 'charming' but means holding something inside.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: electronic mail is one kind of communication.

entries.clue: Skill of political group expelling extremists (3)

indicators.note: The extremists of a word are its end letters, and expelling them throws both out.

blocks.note: PARTY loses its outer letters P and Y

annotation.surface: A political party has a knack for throwing out its radicals.
annotation.walkthrough: "extremists" suggests radical members; here it means the extreme letters of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of craft or knack, as in the art of conversation.

entries.clue: Bedroom items now desired in new style (10)

indicators.note: Letters put in a new style are rearranged into a different form.

annotation.surface: Fashionable bedroom furnishings that are suddenly in demand.
annotation.walkthrough: The home-furnishing surface makes "in new style" sound like fashion talk rather than an instruction to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: these down-filled quilts are things found on a bed.

entries.clue: A Parisian on stone floor (4)

indicators.note: In an across clue, one piece on another comes after it, so the French word follows the abbreviation.

blocks.note: st = stone, the British unit of weight

annotation.surface: A French speaker standing on a stone floor.
annotation.walkthrough: "floor" is a verb: to knock down or astound. A stone is a British weight of 14 pounds, abbreviated st.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym of the verb: flooring someone, with a punch or with news, leaves them dazed.

entries.clue: Publicity material taped, broadcast and modified (7)

indicators.note: To broadcast seed is to scatter it widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order.

annotation.surface: An advert is recorded, aired, then edited.
annotation.walkthrough: "broadcast" fits the media story so well that it passes for its radio sense, not the scattering that tells you to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: altered to suit a new purpose.

entries.clue: Thwarted female told off after game on street (10)

indicators.note: One piece after another is placed later in the answer, so RATED follows the game and street.
In a down clue, one piece on another sits above it, so the game comes before the street.

blocks.note: to rate is an old word for to scold

annotation.surface: A woman is scolded after playing games in the road and feels thwarted.
annotation.walkthrough: RATE meaning 'scold' is old-fashioned but a crossword regular. The order is F, then RATED placed after RU-ST.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean blocked from getting what you were after.

entries.clue: Walking without sure step in short grass and heather (7)

indicators.note: A word that is short has been cut down, so it loses its last letter.

blocks.note: REED, a tall grass, cut short by losing its last letter
ling is another name for heather

annotation.surface: Stumbling through a mix of cropped grass and heather on a moor.
annotation.walkthrough: "short grass" pictures a mown lawn, but it means the word for a grass trimmed by one letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: staggering, the unsteady gait of someone dizzy or drunk.

entries.clue: Both sides welcoming time for drink (5)

indicators.note: To welcome someone is to take them in, so the outer letters take the middle piece inside.

blocks.note: L and R, left and right
a long period of time, placed between the two side letters

annotation.surface: Rival parties come together at closing time for a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: "Both sides" reads like two groups of people; it is the two side letters L and R, left and right.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: this light beer is one kind of drink.

entries.clue: Reddish-orange fabric somehow engrained (9)

indicators.note: Somehow means in some unstated way, so the letters are to be arranged in some other order.

annotation.surface: A reddish cloth where the colour has soaked deep into the weave.
annotation.walkthrough: The word names both a reddish-orange colour and a thin open-weave fabric, so the definition covers both senses at once.
annotation.definitionFit: Two dictionary senses joined: a light gauzy dress fabric, and the colour of pomegranate syrup.

entries.clue: Instant support (6)

blocks.note: a noun: a very short moment
a verb: back a motion at a meeting

annotation.surface: A two-word slogan for help that arrives straight away.
annotation.walkthrough: Read together, the words look like one phrase, but each defines the answer separately, one as a noun and one as a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are everyday: a sixtieth of a minute stands for any instant, and backing a proposal is a verb sense.

entries.clue: Get by with awkward dame, OK? (4,2)

indicators.note: Awkward means clumsy and out of place, so the letters are not in their proper order.

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether they can manage with a difficult older woman.
annotation.walkthrough: "Get by with" looks like the whole definition, but "with" is only the link to the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom matched with an idiom: both phrasal verbs mean managing with limited means.

entries.clue: A new singer on the radio received here? (7)

definitions.text: A new singer on the radio received here?

indicators.note: What is on the radio is heard, not seen, so the singer counts only by how the word sounds.

blocks.note: a tenor is a singer; in a British accent the final R is silent

annotation.surface: Where would a fresh voice heard over the airwaves be picked up?
annotation.walkthrough: The sound match relies on a non-rhotic British accent that drops the final R.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: an aerial is exactly where a singer broadcast on the radio is picked up.

entries.clue: Slow movement initially affecting soldier in bustling activity (6)

indicators.note: Initially means at the start, so only the first letter of 'affecting' is taken.
Pieces placed in something go inside it, so they sit within the word for fuss.

blocks.note: an American soldier; with the A, it goes between the second and third letters of the fuss

annotation.surface: The quiet start of a piece affects a soldier amid all the busy action.
annotation.walkthrough: "movement" suggests the soldier's march, but it is a section of a symphony or concerto.
annotation.definitionFit: A musical term: the Italian tempo marking for 'at ease' names a slow section of a larger work.

entries.clue: Destroy final message at university (3,2)

blocks.note: RIP, rest in peace, the last words on a gravestone
up = in residence at university, as in 'up at Oxford'

annotation.surface: Someone destroys the last note they send while at college.
annotation.walkthrough: Being 'up' means being at university in British usage, the opposite of being sent down.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb for destroying by tearing, as with a letter or a contract.

entries.clue: Earlier leader of religious community (5)

blocks.note: the head of a priory of monks or friars

annotation.surface: A former head of a monastery.
annotation.walkthrough: The two definitions run together like one description of an ex-abbot.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses come from the Latin for 'former' or 'first': the adjective of time, and the title of a monastic superior.

entries.clue: Somehow I daren’t get on the platform? (7)

indicators.note: Somehow means in some unstated way, so the letters are to be arranged in some other order.

annotation.surface: A nervous passenger dares not step out onto the platform.
annotation.walkthrough: "get on" sounds like boarding, but you get on to the platform by leaving the train; the question mark flags the playful definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful definition: stepping off a train is how you end up on the platform.

entries.clue: Examiner’s task is difficult (7)

blocks.note: what an examiner does to candidates
challenging, as in a trying time

annotation.surface: A remark that an examiner's job is a hard one.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a complete sentence, but "is" only links two separate definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the verbal noun for setting exams, and the adjective for something that stretches you.

entries.clue: Rested bottom having expended energy (3)

indicators.note: Something expended has been used up and is gone, so the letter for energy leaves the word.

annotation.surface: Someone sat down to rest after using up all their energy.
annotation.walkthrough: E is the physics symbol for energy.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: taking a seat is one way of resting, and both are past tense.

entries.clue: Arrest slow mover abandoning leader (4)

indicators.note: The leader of a word is its first letter, and abandoning it leaves that letter behind.

annotation.surface: The police catch a sluggish suspect who has left the gang boss behind.
annotation.walkthrough: "leader" reads as a person in charge, but it is the first letter of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: police slang for catching a criminal, as if pinning them down.

entries.clue: Sore I treated inappropriately gets worse (12)

indicators.note: Letters used inappropriately are put in the wrong places, so they must be rearranged.

annotation.surface: A wound handled badly by the speaker becomes worse.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word fits a first-aid mishap, so the fodder hides in plain sight and the surface even agrees with the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from the Latin for 'worse': declining in quality or condition.
